steps.prompt: Two essays about food waste. Which first sentence makes you want to read on?
steps.a: In this essay I am going to write about food waste.
steps.b: Nearly a third of all the food grown in the world is never eaten.
steps.reveal: B is a hook: a surprising fact that makes the reader sit up. A is an announcement: it tells the reader what you’ll do instead of making them care.

cards.title: Five kinds of hook
cards.body: 1. A question: “Have you ever…?”, “What if…?”, “Imagine…”. 2. A surprising fact or number: “Every minute…”. 3. A quote: someone’s words, with who said them. 4. A short story: a tiny true moment, “When I was seven…”. 5. A bold statement: a short, strong claim, “Homework is broken.”

cards.title: Choose a hook that fits
cards.body: Narrative essays love short-story hooks. Informative essays love surprising facts. Argumentative essays love questions and bold statements. Whatever you choose, it must lead to your topic: a hook about sharks doesn’t fit an essay about school lunches.

cards.title: Announce or hook?
cards.telling: Hello! My essay is about why we should have pets in class.
cards.showing: Imagine starting every school day by feeding a hungry hamster.
cards.note: Never “Hello”, “In this essay” or “I am going to tell you”. Start with something that makes the reader curious.

prompts: Which of your three hooks is strongest? Why?
Which kind of hook do you like best when you read?
